Xhosa is a Bantu language spoken in South Africa, most notably by the Xhosa people of the Eastern and Western Cape. It is one of the eleven official languages of South Africa and is among the most well-known languages featuring click consonants, a rare phonetic feature produced by making air suction noises in the mouth, which distinguish it from most other world languages and make it phonetically distinctive and challenging for non-native learners. The language has roughly 8 million native speakers and 11 million second-language speakers. Xhosa features three distinct click consonants: dental, lateral, and palatal, used in ordinary words. As a Bantu or Nguni language, it has an extensive noun class system with gender marked on nouns and triggering agreement on adjectives and verbs. It has a large inventory of consonants including the clicks and a relatively simple vowel system of five vowels. The click consonants are thought to derive from substrate influence from neighboring Khoisan languages, which are primarily click languages, demonstrating the effects of historical language contact. Historically suppressed during the Apartheid era, Xhosa was revitalized as part of post-Apartheid language rights and constitutional protections, making it central to South African linguistic pluralism and post-Apartheid language policy. It belongs to the larger Bantu language family spanning much of sub-Saharan Africa.
